questions.topic: The Living World and Biological Classification
questions.q: The science of identifying, naming and classifying organisms is called
questions.explanation: Taxonomy deals with the characterisation, identification, nomenclature and classification of organisms.

questions.topic: The Living World and Biological Classification
questions.q: A store house of dried, pressed and preserved plant specimens mounted on sheets is called a
questions.explanation: A herbarium preserves plant specimens for study and reference.

questions.topic: The Living World and Biological Classification
questions.q: Which kingdom contains heterotrophic organisms whose cell walls are made of chitin?
questions.explanation: Fungi are heterotrophs with cell walls of chitin and other polysaccharides.

questions.topic: The Living World and Biological Classification
questions.q: The lion (Panthera leo) and the tiger (Panthera tigris) belong to the same
questions.explanation: They share the genus Panthera but are different species.

questions.topic: The Living World and Biological Classification
questions.q: A taxonomic key is arranged as a series of pairs of contrasting characters. Each such pair is called a
questions.explanation: In a key each pair of contrasting statements is a couplet, and each statement is a lead.

questions.topic: The Living World and Biological Classification
questions.q: Potato (Solanum tuberosum) and brinjal (Solanum melongena) are placed in the same
options: genus and family but different species
questions.explanation: Both belong to genus Solanum (and family Solanaceae) but have different species names.

questions.topic: The Living World and Biological Classification
questions.q: Distinguish between a botanical garden and a herbarium.
questions.answer: A botanical garden has living plants grown and labelled for study and display; a herbarium holds dried, pressed and preserved plant specimens on sheets.
questions.explanation: Both are taxonomical aids.

questions.topic: The Living World and Biological Classification
questions.q: Why are scientific names preferred to local names for identifying organisms worldwide?
questions.answer: One organism can have many local names in different regions, and one name may refer to different organisms, causing confusion; a scientific name is unique, universally accepted and follows fixed rules.
keyPoints: Local names vary and cause confusion
Scientific name is unique for each species
questions.explanation: Universal naming is the purpose of nomenclature.

questions.q: The unicellular alga often used as a food supplement by space travellers is
questions.explanation: Chlorella is rich in protein and is used as single-cell protein.

questions.q: Agar, used to grow microbes, is obtained from
questions.explanation: Gelidium and Gracilaria, which are red algae, yield agar.

questions.q: The coralloid roots of Cycas are associated with
questions.explanation: Coralloid roots contain N2-fixing cyanobacteria such as Anabaena.

questions.q: The endosperm formed after double fertilisation in angiosperms is
questions.explanation: Triple fusion of one male gamete with two polar nuclei gives triploid endosperm.

questions.q: Which of the following plants is heterosporous?
questions.explanation: Selaginella produces two kinds of spores, microspores and megaspores.

questions.q: In a moss, the spore germinates to form a green, creeping, branched stage called the
questions.explanation: The protonema is the first stage of the haploid gametophyte of mosses.

questions.q: State two differences between gymnosperms and angiosperms.
questions.answer: Gymnosperms have naked ovules and seeds, no flowers or fruits and no true vessels in the xylem; angiosperms have ovules enclosed in an ovary, bear flowers, form fruits and have vessels.
keyPoints: Flowers and fruits absent or present
Vessels absent or present in xylem
questions.explanation: Angiosperms are the most advanced seed plants.

questions.q: What is alternation of generations? Explain with reference to a fern.
questions.answer: It is the alternation of a diploid sporophytic phase and a haploid gametophytic phase in the life cycle. In a fern the diploid sporophyte bears spores that give a haploid prothallus, which bears gametes whose fusion gives the sporophyte again.
keyPoints: Prothallus makes gametes, zygote gives sporophyte
questions.explanation: Ferns show a diplohaplontic life cycle.

questions.q: The presence of a notochord at some stage of life is a feature of phylum
questions.explanation: Notochord, dorsal hollow nerve cord and pharyngeal gill slits characterise chordates.

questions.q: Which of the following has a cartilaginous endoskeleton?
questions.explanation: Scoliodon (dogfish) belongs to Chondrichthyes, the cartilaginous fishes.

questions.q: Metamerism, the division of the body into similar segments, is seen in phylum
questions.explanation: Earthworms and leeches show metameric segmentation.

questions.q: Which feature is found only in class Mammalia?
questions.explanation: Mammary glands for suckling the young are unique to mammals; birds also have four-chambered hearts.

questions.q: An animal has a chitinous exoskeleton, jointed legs, a body divided into head, thorax and abdomen, and sheds its exoskeleton periodically. It belongs to
questions.explanation: Arthropods, such as insects, have a chitinous cuticle that is moulted.

questions.q: A soft-bodied animal with a calcareous shell, a muscular foot, a mantle and a rasping organ called the radula belongs to
questions.explanation: Radula, mantle and muscular foot are features of Mollusca, e.g. snail and Pila.

questions.q: Write two differences between cartilaginous fishes and bony fishes.
questions.answer: Cartilaginous fishes (Chondrichthyes) have a cartilage endoskeleton, placoid scales, no air bladder and gill slits without an operculum; bony fishes (Osteichthyes) have a bony skeleton, cycloid or ctenoid scales, an air bladder and an operculum covering the gills.
keyPoints: Operculum and air bladder absent or present
questions.explanation: These are the two classes of fishes.

questions.q: Why is class Amphibia so named? Mention two features of an amphibian.
questions.answer: Amphibians can live both in water and on land. They have moist skin without scales, a three-chambered heart, and respire through gills, lungs and skin.
keyPoints: Live in water and on land
questions.explanation: The name comes from the Greek for 'double life'.

questions.topic: Morphology and Anatomy of Flowering Plants
questions.q: The male reproductive whorl of a flower is called the
questions.explanation: The androecium consists of stamens, each with an anther and a filament.

questions.topic: Morphology and Anatomy of Flowering Plants
questions.q: The mango fruit is an example of a
questions.explanation: A mango has a fleshy mesocarp and a hard stony endocarp, so it is a drupe.

questions.topic: Morphology and Anatomy of Flowering Plants
questions.q: In dicot leaves the guard cells of stomata are
questions.explanation: Guard cells are bean (kidney) shaped in dicots and dumb-bell shaped in grasses.

questions.topic: Morphology and Anatomy of Flowering Plants
questions.q: Living cells with thickened corners due to deposition of cellulose, hemicellulose and pectin that give mechanical support form
questions.explanation: Collenchyma is a living supporting tissue, found below the epidermis of dicot stems.

questions.topic: Morphology and Anatomy of Flowering Plants
questions.q: A transverse section of a stem shows scattered vascular bundles, each closed and surrounded by a sclerenchymatous sheath. The stem belongs to
questions.explanation: Scattered, closed bundles with a sclerenchymatous sheath are typical of monocot stems such as maize.

questions.topic: Morphology and Anatomy of Flowering Plants
questions.q: In a flower the ovary is placed above the other floral parts, which arise from below it. This condition is
questions.explanation: Hypogynous flowers (mustard, brinjal) have a superior ovary.

questions.topic: Morphology and Anatomy of Flowering Plants
questions.q: Distinguish between the anatomy of a dorsiventral (dicot) leaf and an isobilateral (monocot) leaf.
questions.answer: A dicot leaf has differentiated palisade and spongy mesophyll and more stomata on the lower surface; a monocot leaf has undifferentiated mesophyll, similar stomata on both surfaces and bulliform cells in the upper epidermis.
keyPoints: Stomata mostly lower or on both surfaces
questions.explanation: These differences are seen in transverse sections.

questions.topic: Morphology and Anatomy of Flowering Plants
questions.q: Why is the heartwood of an old tree dark in colour and unable to conduct water?
questions.answer: In heartwood the xylem elements are filled with tannins, resins, gums and oils and their lumens are blocked by tyloses. It is hard, durable and resistant to microbes, and provides mechanical support but no water conduction.
questions.explanation: Sapwood, the outer region, conducts water.

questions.q: The tissue that stores fat in the body is
questions.explanation: Adipose tissue is a loose connective tissue rich in fat-storing cells.

questions.q: Which blood cells help in the clotting of blood?
questions.explanation: Platelets (thrombocytes) release substances that trigger clotting.

questions.q: A frog can absorb oxygen directly through its moist
questions.explanation: Cutaneous respiration through the skin is used in water and during hibernation.

questions.q: The excretory organs of a cockroach are
questions.explanation: Malpighian tubules at the junction of the midgut and hindgut remove nitrogenous waste.

questions.q: In a male frog, the duct that carries both sperms and urine to the cloaca is the
questions.explanation: The ureter acts as a urinogenital duct in the male frog.

questions.q: The walls of the lung alveoli and blood capillaries are lined with simple squamous epithelium mainly because the thin flat cells
options: help in diffusion of gases and other substances
questions.explanation: A thin one-cell layer favours rapid diffusion and filtration.

questions.q: Write three differences between skeletal muscle and smooth muscle.
questions.answer: Skeletal muscle is striated, multinucleate and voluntary, attached to bones; smooth muscle is non-striated, uninucleate, spindle shaped and involuntary, found in walls of hollow organs.
questions.explanation: Cardiac muscle is striated but involuntary.

questions.q: A cockroach has no respiratory pigment in its blood, yet its cells get enough oxygen. Explain.
questions.answer: Air enters through spiracles into a network of tracheae and tracheoles that carry oxygen directly to the tissues, so the haemolymph does not need to transport oxygen.
questions.explanation: Insect respiration is by a tracheal system.

questions.q: The term 'cell' was first used by
questions.explanation: Robert Hooke observed cork cells in 1665 and called them cells.

questions.q: The statement that new cells arise from pre-existing cells was made by
questions.explanation: Virchow stated 'omnis cellula-e cellula', modifying the cell theory.

questions.q: The main component of the plant cell wall is
questions.explanation: Plant cell walls are made mainly of cellulose, hemicellulose and pectins.

questions.q: Which organelles, containing hydrolytic enzymes, are called 'suicide bags'?
questions.explanation: Lysosomes may burst and digest the cell if their enzymes leak out.

questions.q: Which of the following cell components is NOT bounded by a membrane?
questions.explanation: Ribosomes are made of RNA and protein and have no limiting membrane.

questions.q: The inner membrane of a mitochondrion is folded into cristae. This increases
options: the surface area for the enzymes of oxidative phosphorylation
questions.explanation: More inner membrane carries more electron transport components and ATP synthase.

questions.q: Distinguish between passive transport and active transport across the cell membrane.
questions.answer: Passive transport moves substances down the concentration gradient without using energy, as in diffusion; active transport moves substances against the gradient using ATP, as in the sodium-potassium pump.
questions.explanation: Carrier proteins are involved in active transport.

questions.q: A plant cell and an animal cell are placed in pure water. Predict and explain what happens to each.
questions.answer: Water enters both by osmosis. The plant cell becomes turgid but does not burst because the rigid cell wall resists expansion; the animal cell has no wall, so it swells and may burst.
questions.explanation: Pure water is hypotonic to the cell contents.

questions.q: The most abundant protein in the animal world is
questions.explanation: Collagen is the most abundant protein in animals, while RuBisCO is the most abundant in the biosphere.

questions.q: The reserve carbohydrate in animals is
questions.explanation: Glycogen is stored mainly in the liver and muscles.

questions.q: Enzymes that catalyse the joining of two compounds, using energy from ATP, belong to the class
questions.explanation: Ligases join substrates, usually with ATP hydrolysis.

questions.q: A nucleoside consists of
options: a nitrogenous base and a phosphate group
a sugar and a phosphate group
a nitrogenous base and a pentose sugar
questions.explanation: Adding a phosphate group to a nucleoside gives a nucleotide.

questions.q: Zinc is a cofactor required for the activity of the enzyme
questions.explanation: Carboxypeptidase needs Zn2+ as a cofactor.

questions.q: A sample of double-stranded DNA contains 30 per cent adenine. What percentage of guanine does it contain?
questions.explanation: A = T = 30 per cent, so G + C = 40 per cent, i.e. G = 20 per cent.

questions.q: What is a prosthetic group? Give one example.
questions.answer: A prosthetic group is an organic non-protein part tightly bound to the apoenzyme, needed for activity. Example: haem in the enzymes peroxidase and catalase.
keyPoints: Tightly bound to the enzyme protein
Example: haem in peroxidase or catalase
questions.explanation: Prosthetic groups, coenzymes and metal ions are all cofactors.

questions.q: Explain how changes in pH affect the activity of an enzyme.
questions.answer: Each enzyme works best at an optimum pH. Away from it, the charges on the amino acids of the active site change, altering the shape of the protein, so substrate binding falls and activity decreases.
keyPoints: Extreme pH changes charge and shape
questions.explanation: For example pepsin works at acid pH and trypsin at alkaline pH.

questions.q: The inactive stage in which cells exit the cell cycle and no longer divide is called
questions.explanation: Cells in G0 remain metabolically active but do not proliferate.

questions.q: Chromosomes line up at the equatorial plate during
questions.explanation: In metaphase chromosomes are aligned at the equator with spindle fibres attached to their kinetochores.

questions.q: In a typical human cell that divides once in about 24 hours, the duration of mitosis (M phase) is only about
questions.explanation: Mitosis is short, about an hour; most of the cycle is spent in interphase.

questions.q: The nuclear envelope reappears and chromosomes decondense during
questions.explanation: Telophase is the reverse of prophase in these events.

questions.q: Which of the following distinguishes anaphase I of meiosis from anaphase of mitosis?
options: Homologous chromosomes, not sister chromatids, separate
questions.explanation: In anaphase I whole homologous chromosomes move to opposite poles; the centromeres do not split.

questions.q: A somatic cell with 8 chromosomes divides by mitosis. Each daughter cell will have
questions.explanation: Mitosis is equational, so the chromosome number is the same as in the parent cell.

questions.q: Describe the main events of prophase of mitosis.
questions.answer: Chromatin condenses into chromosomes made of two chromatids; the centrioles move to opposite poles and the spindle starts to form; the nucleolus and nuclear envelope begin to disappear.
questions.explanation: Prophase follows the G2 phase.

questions.q: Compare anaphase I and anaphase II of meiosis.
questions.answer: In anaphase I homologous chromosomes, each with two chromatids, separate and go to opposite poles; in anaphase II the centromeres divide and sister chromatids separate, as in mitosis.
keyPoints: Centromere divides only in anaphase II
questions.explanation: Reduction in chromosome number takes place in meiosis I.

questions.q: Joseph Priestley's experiments with a mint plant and a candle showed that plants
options: restore to the air whatever burning candles remove
questions.explanation: Priestley concluded plants restore the air, later shown to be oxygen.

questions.q: The final hydrogen acceptor of the light reaction of photosynthesis is
questions.explanation: NADP+ is reduced to NADPH in the light reaction.

questions.q: The reaction centre chlorophyll a of photosystem I absorbs light best at a wavelength of
questions.explanation: PS I has P700, and PS II has P680.

questions.q: For fixing each molecule of CO2, the Calvin cycle requires
questions.explanation: Three ATP and two NADPH are used per CO2 fixed.

questions.q: How many turns of the Calvin cycle are required to synthesise one molecule of glucose?
questions.explanation: One CO2 is fixed per turn and glucose has six carbons.

questions.q: The rate of photosynthesis does not increase when light intensity is raised, because CO2 concentration is very low. This illustrates
questions.explanation: Blackman's law says the factor in shortest supply limits the rate.

questions.q: Explain the chemiosmotic hypothesis of ATP synthesis in chloroplasts.
questions.answer: Photolysis of water and electron transport pump protons into the thylakoid lumen, building a proton gradient across the membrane. Protons flow back to the stroma through ATP synthase, which uses the energy to make ATP from ADP and Pi.
keyPoints: Proton gradient built in thylakoid lumen
ATP made from ADP and Pi
questions.explanation: The same principle operates in mitochondria.

questions.q: What is photorespiration and why is it considered wasteful?
questions.answer: In photorespiration RuBisCO binds O2 instead of CO2 in the presence of high oxygen and low CO2, so RuBP is oxidised and CO2 is released. It produces neither ATP nor NADPH and reduces sugar synthesis.
keyPoints: No ATP or NADPH made, reduces yield
questions.explanation: C3 plants lose a part of fixed carbon this way.

questions.q: The Krebs cycle takes place in the
questions.explanation: The enzymes of the TCA cycle are located in the mitochondrial matrix.

questions.q: The Krebs cycle starts with the condensation of acetyl CoA with
questions.explanation: Acetyl CoA joins oxaloacetic acid to form citric acid.

questions.q: Oxidative phosphorylation, the synthesis of ATP in respiration, occurs by the enzyme ATP synthase located in the
questions.explanation: ATP synthase (complex V) is in the inner mitochondrial membrane.

questions.q: In one turn of the Krebs cycle, the number of NADH molecules formed is
questions.explanation: One turn gives 3 NADH, 1 FADH2 and 1 GTP (or ATP), and releases 2 CO2.

questions.q: How many CO2 molecules are released when one glucose molecule is completely oxidised, starting from glycolysis through the Krebs cycle?
questions.explanation: Each pyruvate gives 3 CO2 (1 in the link reaction, 2 in the cycle), so two pyruvate give 6.

questions.q: Complete oxidation of tripalmitin uses 72.5 molecules of O2 and releases 51 molecules of CO2. Its respiratory quotient is about
What is the role of oxygen in aerobic respiration?
questions.answer: Oxygen acts as the final acceptor of electrons and protons in the electron transport chain, forming water; this lets NADH and FADH2 be reoxidised so that ATP production can continue.
keyPoints: Keeps electron transport and ATP synthesis going
questions.explanation: Without oxygen the electron transport chain stops.

questions.q: Why is the respiratory pathway described as amphibolic?
questions.answer: It involves both breakdown (catabolism) of carbohydrates, fats and proteins to release energy, and the supply of intermediates such as acetyl CoA and organic acids that are used to synthesise fatty acids and amino acids.
questions.explanation: Amphibolic pathways serve both catabolic and anabolic functions.

questions.q: The growth movement of a plant part towards light is called
questions.explanation: Shoots bend towards light, showing positive phototropism.

questions.q: The process by which cells derived from meristems become specialised for specific functions is
questions.explanation: Differentiation produces structurally and functionally distinct cell types.

questions.q: The response of flowering to the relative duration of day and night is called
questions.explanation: Photoperiodism classifies plants as short-day, long-day or day-neutral.

questions.q: In the sigmoid growth curve, the phase in which growth is fastest is the
questions.explanation: In the log phase the growth rate increases rapidly.

questions.q: Which combination correctly describes the role of two hormones in seed dormancy?
options: Gibberellin induces dormancy and ABA breaks it
ABA induces dormancy and gibberellin breaks it
Ethylene breaks dormancy and auxin induces it
questions.explanation: ABA maintains dormancy; gibberellins promote germination.

questions.q: Seedless fruits can be produced without fertilisation, a process called parthenocarpy, by spraying flowers with
questions.explanation: Auxins and gibberellins can induce parthenocarpy, e.g. in tomatoes.

questions.q: Distinguish between differentiation, dedifferentiation and redifferentiation.
questions.answer: Differentiation: cells from meristems become specialised. Dedifferentiation: living differentiated cells regain the capacity to divide, as in cambium formation. Redifferentiation: such cells lose the ability to divide again and mature for specific functions.
keyPoints: Redifferentiation: mature again for a function
questions.explanation: Interfascicular cambium arises by dedifferentiation.

questions.q: Ethephon, a compound that releases ethylene, is widely used in agriculture. Give three uses and explain the reasoning.
questions.answer: Ethylene hastens fruit ripening (tomato, apple), promotes flowering in pineapple so that fruits form together, and promotes female flowers in cucumbers, increasing yield; it also causes abscission of leaves and fruits.
questions.explanation: Ethylene is a gaseous plant hormone.

questions.q: The largest gland in the human body is the
questions.explanation: The liver weighs about 1.2 to 1.5 kg in an adult.

questions.q: The muscular partition separating the thoracic cavity from the abdominal cavity is the
questions.explanation: Contraction of the diaphragm increases the thoracic volume in inspiration.

questions.q: The total number of permanent teeth in an adult human is
questions.explanation: The dental formula 2123/2123 gives 32 teeth.

questions.q: The average lifespan of a human red blood cell is about
questions.explanation: RBCs live about 120 days and are destroyed in the spleen.

questions.q: A person with blood group AB is a universal recipient because the plasma of this group
options: has both anti-A and anti-B antibodies
has no anti-A or anti-B antibodies
questions.explanation: Group AB has A and B antigens on RBCs and no anti-A or anti-B antibodies in plasma.

questions.q: Erythroblastosis foetalis can occur when
options: an Rh positive mother carries an Rh negative foetus
an Rh negative mother carries an Rh positive foetus
both parents have blood group O
questions.explanation: Rh antibodies of an Rh-negative mother can cross the placenta and attack the red cells of an Rh-positive foetus in a later pregnancy.

questions.q: Calculate the cardiac output of a person whose stroke volume is 70 mL and heart rate is 72 beats per minute.
questions.answer: Cardiac output = stroke volume x heart rate = 70 mL x 72 = 5040 mL per minute, about 5 litres per minute.
keyPoints: Cardiac output = stroke volume x heart rate
questions.explanation: The average human cardiac output is about 5 litres per minute.

questions.q: Explain which features make the alveoli efficient sites for exchange of gases.
questions.answer: The alveoli have very thin walls of squamous epithelium, a very large combined surface area, and a rich network of capillaries, so oxygen and carbon dioxide diffuse rapidly across a short distance.
questions.explanation: Each lung has millions of alveoli.

questions.q: The main nitrogenous waste excreted by humans is
questions.explanation: Humans are ureotelic; urea is formed in the liver.

questions.q: The number of bones in the adult human skeleton is
questions.explanation: The adult human skeleton has 206 bones.

questions.q: The joint at the shoulder is an example of a
questions.explanation: The shoulder and hip are ball and socket joints, allowing movement in many directions.

questions.q: The gland called the master gland because it controls other endocrine glands is the
questions.explanation: The pituitary secretes tropic hormones that control other glands.

questions.q: Enlargement of the thyroid gland, called simple goitre, is caused by
options: deficiency of iodine in the diet
questions.explanation: Lack of iodine reduces thyroid hormone production and the gland enlarges.

questions.q: Nerve impulses travel faster in myelinated nerve fibres because the impulse
options: jumps from one node of Ranvier to the next
questions.explanation: Myelin insulates the axon, so depolarisation occurs only at the nodes (saltatory conduction).

questions.q: Which hormones regulate blood calcium levels? State the action of each.
questions.answer: Parathyroid hormone raises blood Ca2+ by increasing its release from bone and reabsorption in kidneys; calcitonin from the thyroid lowers blood Ca2+ by reducing bone resorption.
questions.explanation: The two hormones act in opposite ways.

questions.q: Why does a nerve impulse pass across a chemical synapse in only one direction?
questions.answer: Neurotransmitter vesicles are present only in the axon terminal of the pre-synaptic neuron and receptors only on the post-synaptic membrane, so the transmitter can act only in one direction.
keyPoints: Neurotransmitter stored in the pre-synaptic terminal
questions.explanation: This ensures orderly transmission of information.
